procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 31.05.2016 of the High Court of Karnataka at Bengaluru in CRLA No.245 of 2011.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant (Shiva Kumar) preferred an appeal before the High Court to challenge the conviction and sentence imposed by the Sessions Judge. The State Government also preferred an appeal for enhancement of the sentence. The High Court dismissed both appeals.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant approached the Supreme Court. On 21st April 2017, the Supreme Court issued notice limited to the issue of the sentence.

directions: The order of sentence of the Trial Court for the offence punishable under Section 302 of the IPC is modified.
The appellant shall undergo imprisonment for life.
The appellant shall be released only after he completes thirty years of actual sentence.

issue.issue_text: Whether the sentence imposed on the appellant for the offence punishable under Section 302 of the IPC should be modified.

facts: The appellant was convicted for offences including murder under Section 302 of the IPC.
The Trial Court sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment for the rest of his life.
The High Court upheld this sentence.
The appeal to the Supreme Court was limited to the issue of the sentence.

The appellant argued that at the time of the offence, he was 22, had a family, no criminal history, and had shown good conduct in jail, including earning a B.A. degree. He had already served over 17 years.
law: The appellant's counsel, citing the Constitution Bench case of *Union of India v. V. Sriharan*, argued that a modified sentence (like imprisonment for the entirety of life or a fixed term) can only be imposed by a High Court or the Supreme Court when commuting a death penalty.
The State argued that Constitutional Courts have the power to impose such modified sentences based on the gravity of the offence, even if the death penalty was not originally imposed.

The Supreme Court clarified the law laid down in the *V. Sriharan* case. It held that the power to impose a modified punishment (imprisonment for life without remission or for a specific term over 14 years) can be exercised only by the High Court and the Supreme Court, not by a Trial Court.

Crucially, the Court also held that this power is not restricted to cases where a death sentence is being commuted. Constitutional Courts can impose a fixed-term sentence even in cases where capital punishment was not imposed.
application: Applying the law, the Court first determined that the Trial Court had erred by imposing a sentence of imprisonment for the "rest of his life," as it lacked the authority to impose such a modified sentence.
The Supreme Court then affirmed its own authority to impose a modified, fixed-term sentence in this case.

The Court balanced the aggravating and mitigating circumstances. It considered the brutality of the crime and the need to maintain public confidence in the justice system, while also noting the appellant's potential for reformation.
Considering all these factors, including the rights of the victim, the Court concluded that this was an appropriate case to exercise its power to impose a special, modified punishment.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the appellant's plea to modify the sentence. It set aside the Trial Court's sentence and directed that the appellant shall undergo imprisonment for life but shall be released only after completing thirty years of actual sentence.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the sentence imposed on the appellant for the offence punishable under Section 302 of the IPC should be modified.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued, citing the Swamy Shraddananda case, that a fixed-term or modified sentence can only be imposed as a substitute for the death penalty.
respondent_arguments: The respondent (State) argued that Constitutional Courts have the power to impose modified sentences based on the gravity of the offense and other factors, even when the death penalty has not been imposed.
The respondent contended that this power should not be restricted only to cases involving the commutation of a death sentence.
The respondent asserted that the facts of this specific case justified the stringent sentence of imprisonment for the entirety of the appellant's life, as imposed by the High Court.

cases.case_name: Union of India v. V. Sriharan alias Murugan & Ors.
cases.principle: The holding of a Constitution Bench cannot be construed in a narrow perspective.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The power to impose a modified punishment, such as a fixed-term sentence or imprisonment for the convict's natural life as an alternative to the death penalty, can be exercised only by the High Court and the Supreme Court, and not by any inferior court.
obiter: What is held by the Constitution Bench, cannot be construed in a narrow perspective.
We think that it is time that the course suggested in Dalbir Singh [(1979) 3 SCC 745 : 1979 SCC (Cri) 848] should receive a formal recognition by the Court.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: A Constitutional Court must exercise the power of imposing a special category of modified punishment by considering all attending circumstances. This includes balancing the possibility of reformation of the accused against the need to avoid undue leniency in a brutal case, which would adversely affect public confidence in the legal system, and also considering the rights of the victim. Based on these factors, the court determined that a fixed-term sentence of thirty years was appropriate in this case.
legal_tests_applied: The court must conduct a balancing of aggravating and mitigating circumstances to determine if a special category of modified punishment is warranted.

The power of a Constitutional Court to impose a fixed-term or modified sentence is not restricted to only being a substitute for the death penalty, as established by the Constitution Bench in Union of India v. V. Sriharan.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument that a fixed-term sentence can only be imposed as a substitute for the death penalty was rejected, as the court held that the power of Constitutional Courts, as affirmed by the Constitution Bench in V. Sriharan, cannot be construed in such a narrow perspective.
why_respondent_won: The court accepted the respondent's position that a Constitutional Court has the power to impose a special category of modified punishment based on the specific facts and circumstances of a case, even when the death penalty has not been imposed.
policy_considerations: Showing undue leniency in such a brutal case will adversely affect the public confidence in the efficacy of the legal system.
The Court must consider the rights of the victim as well.
